stories.title: Saving 100 terabytes of memory by optimizing 1.1.1.1's DNS cache
stories.author: TangerineDream

topComments.author: eviks
topComments.text: > Once we store a DNS response in the cache, however, we never modify it again. The capacity field serves no purpose, but still costs 8 bytes per Vec Were there no design discussions/reviews when the system was setup to catch trivial things like this?

topComments.author: irdc
topComments.text: This is why system programming still matters. Looks like they're missing the obvious optimisation of putting the record data right after the CacheEntry members instead of allocating memory separately though. But that might just be me as a C-programmer talking and not be all that easy in Rust.

topComments.author: strenholme
topComments.text: With my own MaraDNS, I aggressively optimized the memory usage of blacklist entries by having a single really big malloc() to allocate the memory for the entries, then traversing that memory block for potentially blacklisted entries. When I was using one malloc() per entry, a large blacklist took up 237 megabytes of memory. The same blacklist, once optimized to be loaded with a single malloc() call, only took up 9.5 megabytes of memory. https://samboy.github.io/blog/entries/MaraDNS.html#BlogEntry...

topComments.author: OptionOfT
topComments.text: > we store the records as a single Box<[u8]> containing each record encoded as a 2-byte length prefix followed by its raw bytes. Interestingly this is exactly how netlink works-ish: https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/focal/man3/netlink.3.ht... You start, get the type & length, and then that is how many bytes you read. Some issues with that when you deserialize, from a raw stream in to `[u8; 4096]` buffer, the alignment is only guaranteed to be on 1 byte, not 4 bytes. In practice it is 4 bytes, but if you run those tests with Miri, you'll get yelled at. So the fix there is to declare the buffer with a type that mandates the alignment of the largest type that you're going to be deserializing. So then you start your buffer as follows: `[u32; 1024]`, and with `slice::from_raw_parts` you get to turn that into `[u8; 4096]` with the expected alignment. As an exercise I wrote a streaming parser for netlink, the current existing package serializes everything, all at once.

stories.summary: Cloudflare optimized the DNS cache for its 1.1.1.1 service and achieved a massive 100 terabyte memory reduction through engineering improvements. The article details the technical optimizations made to improve performance and efficiency of one of the world's largest public DNS resolvers.

The author argues that while frontier models will remain essential for breakthrough work, the real opportunity lies in deploying "fast/cheap/good-enough" models for responsive, routine tasks that comprise the majority of business work. This shift in model economics could finally unlock the consumer AI startup market that has been constrained by high token costs.

topComments.author: nater5000
topComments.text: I was pleasantly surprised when I attempted to scroll down and realized everything the author wanted to present fit on-screen. It's almost ironic that this site is able to make such an obvious, compelling presentation without being overly verbose or complicated (something which LLMs have a hard time doing). I wouldn't read TOO deeply into what is being presented, but the author has done a good job to not inject their own bias into the presentation which works well. I suspect, as we continue forward, humans will slowly start to adopt the language of LLMs, or at least certain language quirks that come from interacting with LLMs. Something I've noticed in my own writing is that I now present lists of examples in a consistent way: "... such as <example 1>, <example 2>, etc., ...". I started to notice I was using this pattern quite a bit somewhat recently, but I took a quick look at some of my social media posts and realized it's been occurring for a while. I had realized that I grown accustomed to this kind of language because, especially early on, LLMs would focus too much on the specific examples I'd provide when, really, I was just trying to give them a sense of what I was looking for. I just picked up that providing two examples then adding the "etc." worked to get the LLM to not focus so much on the specific examples and to understand that they need to consider more than what I explicitly presented. Of course, now I write like that in my social media comments, in Slack with my colleagues, etc. :> I'd be interested to see if anyone can identify trends like this, since I think the human-language component of the adoption of LLMs is probably being somewhat neglected despite probably being surely dramatically affected.

stories.summary: Suica is Japan's pioneering IC transit card developed in the 1990s that revolutionized train travel by enabling tap-based transactions processed in milliseconds without batteries or internet connectivity. The article traces Suica's development from Sony's initial FeliCa technology rejection by JR East, through successful implementation in Hong Kong, to its eventual adoption in Japan as a solution to modernize stations and reduce congestion. stories.summary: Anthropic is launching a research preview of the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that allows AI agents to safely operate multiple lab and manufacturing devices in parallel by standardizing how different instruments communicate and receive commands. MHS dramatically reduces hardware integration time from weeks or months to hours or minutes, while enabling AI agents to autonomously orchestrate complex experiments, monitor results in real-time, and recover from errors without human intervention. The standard is being shared with research labs and manufacturers across multiple fields to develop safety practices before being made open source.

stories.summary: This article discusses how centralized social media platforms like X have progressively closed their APIs and restricted third-party access, using Nitter's cease-and-desist letter as an example of this trend. The author argues that true interoperability requires shared database access rather than limited APIs, and presents atproto as an emerging solution built on personal data servers and data replication to create a more open internet. The piece advocates for a decentralized approach to social networking that prioritizes user freedom and data portability over corporate control.

stories.summary: Terminal-Bench-Science is a new benchmark that evaluates AI agents on real scientific research workflows contributed by practicing scientists across multiple disciplines, with the goal of developing AI assistants that can handle technical tasks and accelerate scientific discovery. In the first release, 70 expert-curated tasks across life, physical, Earth, mathematical, and engineering sciences show that the strongest model (Claude Opus 5) achieves only a 30% resolution rate, indicating significant room for AI progress. The benchmark is designed as a continuous, evolving platform that creates feedback between scientific community needs and AI development, rather than a one-time publication.
